sets.marsfield: Mars surface. Butterscotch haze sky fading to dusty pink at the horizon, a small pale Sun, rust-orange rocky plain with 4 px outlined rocks and faint wheel tracks, soft warm rim light; setp.t 0..1 = slow camera drift and drifting dust; setp.dust 0..1 = a dust gust; setp.dark 0..1 = the light dims to dusk and stars show; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.mcc: Mission control room. far: wall of big dark screens with soft blue charts and one big world map; mid: two rows of desks with laptops, coffee mugs and a sticky note; near: dark chair silhouettes; setp.alert 0..1 = the screens flash amber; setp.calm 0..1 = amber fades to green; setp.t 0..1 = slow push through the room.
sets.heartbeat: Heartbeat monitor. Deep-navy bg, a big outlined screen with a bright cyan ECG trace sweeping left to right, one tall blip every 4 seconds drawn as a spike; setp.t 0..1 = the trace sweeps; setp.missed 0..25 = small red tick marks count missed beats under the line and the trace goes flat; setp.glow 'cyan'|'red'|'gold'.
sets.relay: Mars to Earth relay diagram. Deep-navy bg; a rust Mars ball with a tiny rover at the lower left, a small orbiter above it, a blue Earth with a dish at the far right; thin cyan lines; setp.t 0..1 = pulses travel; setp.relay 0..1 = the short fast route rover->orbiter->Earth glows thick; setp.direct 0..1 = a thin slow direct line rover->Earth glows gold; setp.cut 0..1 = the relay line breaks with a small red spark; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.wheels: Spacecraft reaction wheels diagram. Deep-navy bg; a small gold-and-grey orbiter body in the middle with four outlined wheels in a 2x2 grid beside it, labelled 1-4; setp.t 0..1 = the wheels spin; setp.dead 0..2 = wheel 1 (2013) then wheel 2 (2026) darken with red crosses; setp.need 0..1 = a cream bracket 'AT LEAST 3' appears; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'|'red'.
sets.fuel: Fuel gauge. Deep-navy bg; a big round outlined tank with a visible liquid level and a calendar strip beside it; setp.frac 0..1 = liquid level; setp.t 0..1 = the level slowly drains; setp.range 0..1 = a cream bracket marks 1 to 2 months; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'|'red'.
sets.orbiter: Odyssey in orbit. Deep-navy bg; the curve of a rust Mars filling the lower half, a small gold-and-grey orbiter with two solar wings above it; setp.t 0..1 = the orbiter glides across and tiny stars drift; setp.tilt 0..1 = it slowly tumbles away from the Sun; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'|'red'.
sets.timeline: A horizontal timeline. Deep-navy bg; a long gold line with milestone dots and cream calendar tags; setp.t 0..1 = the camera pans along the line; setp.now 0..1 = a bright cyan marker glides along; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.landers: Four landing sites on a Mars globe. Deep-navy bg; a big rust Mars globe with four small outlined pins labelled PHOENIX, SPIRIT, OPPORTUNITY, CURIOSITY and a tiny orbiter circling; setp.t 0..1 = slow globe turn; setp.send 0..1 = cyan lines from each pin to the orbiter glow in turn; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props._probe_old: Icon of the BepiColombo stack: a small gold-foil box body with two dark solar-panel wings, a round grey antenna dish and a silver conical sunshield on top, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds an orange thruster flame at the bottom.
props.thermo: Tall outlined thermometer, cream glass tube, red or blue fluid to pp.frac (0..1), pp.label text beneath in FONTS.ui; pp.color red|cyan.
props.rover: Icon of the Perseverance rover: boxy cream-grey body, six dark wheels, a thin mast with a camera head and a round white high-gain dish on the deck, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a soft cyan bloom; pp.dim true greys it out.
props.radio: Small outlined radio box, dark #1E1B2E body with a cream front, a tiny antenna and an LED; pp.led green|red|amber sets the light, pp.half true shows a half-full signal meter; pp.s scale.
props.heart: Round outlined badge with a small cream heart and a tiny cyan pulse ring that beats once a second; pp.flat true freezes it to a flat grey line; pp.s scale.
props.dish: Outlined Deep Space Network dish on a short pedestal, cream bowl, small cyan signal arcs; pp.s scale; pp.glow true pulses the arcs.
props.wheel: Round outlined reaction wheel: grey disc with spokes and a gold hub, 4 px outline; pp.spin true spins it, pp.dead true makes it dark with a small red cross; pp.s scale.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back, arms loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation across the shot while looking around.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point up at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

chapters.title: THE END
chapters.sub: Back by the end of November

film.vo: For one hundred seconds, a rover on Mars heard nothing.
Its own radio had gone quiet.
And the brain on board noticed every missing beat.
Twenty-five in a row, and it pulled the plug.
This is NASA's Perseverance, and it is still in trouble today.
So what if you were the one stuck inside it?
Here is the rule. Your radio must say hello to your brain.
A little ping, again and again, about every four seconds.
Each ping resets a counter inside the main computer.
Ping, reset. Ping, reset. You barely notice it.
But if the pings stop, the counter keeps climbing.
Hit the limit, and the computer assumes the radio is dead.
Thirty October. Your alarm goes off, you power on for the day.
Your main radio is supposed to wake up with you.
It doesn't send a single ping.
One missed. Then five. Then ten.
You can't feel it, but your computer is counting.
At twenty-five, that is about a hundred seconds of silence.
Your computer does not panic. It follows a script.
Step one. Power off the radio that stopped talking.
Step two. Swap to the backup radio, an identical twin.
Step three. Shut everything non-essential down. Safe mode.
Cameras off. Arm still. Wheels still. You wait.
Ground teams on Earth bring the rover back out of it.
Good news. You're awake, and the backup radio works.
Then the engineers read the data, and find a second problem.
The backup is only transmitting at about half its expected power.
So now both radios are in doubt.
NASA stops using either one until it is sure they're safe.
A radio you cannot trust is worse than silence.
So how do you talk to Earth with no relay radio?
Normally, your radios hand data up to an orbiter overhead.
The orbiter has a big dish and a quick path to Earth.
That is the fast lane for pictures, and lots of them.
With both relay radios parked, you have one option left.
Shout straight at Earth, using your big white dish.
It is called the high-gain antenna, on the X-band.
NASA's Deep Space Network dishes on Earth listen for you.
The catch. The data rate is significantly lower.
It is like going from fibre broadband to a dial-up modem.
So you do the sensible thing. You save the bandwidth.
Everything left in the pipe goes to diagnostics. Not science.
Science and instrument work are paused.
No new pictures. The raw image feed on the website goes quiet.
For a camera-mad rover, that is a very long weekend.
And the rover is not the only machine in trouble.
Meet Mars Odyssey, the orbiter that carries the rover's mail.
It launched in April two thousand one.
It reached Mars orbit that October.
It was designed to work for just over two and a half years.
It has now orbited Mars for twenty-five years.
Longer than any other mission has ever worked at the Red Planet.
It mapped the whole surface, and found buried ice a metre down.
It also relayed the first pictures from four landers.
Phoenix. Spirit. Opportunity. Curiosity.
So when Odyssey stumbles, the whole Mars network feels it.
Between the fourth and sixth of November, Odyssey went into safe mode.
Engineers found a reaction wheel had stopped spinning.
Think of reaction wheels as the spacecraft's steering.
Speed one up or slow it down, and the whole craft turns.
That keeps its solar panels pointed at the Sun.
Odyssey carries four wheels.
One of them already died back in twenty thirteen.
Now a second one has stopped. That leaves two.
And the rule is simple. You need at least three.
Without three, you steer with thrusters alone.
Thrusters burn hydrazine, and Odyssey has been up there a long time.
After twenty-five years, the tank is far from full.
The team estimates enough fuel to steer alone for one to two months.
That is a clock, and nobody can pause it.
They are still refining that estimate, so the number could move.
Meanwhile the rover's backup mail carrier is limping.
Two sick machines, on one planet, in the same fortnight.
Remember the heartbeat? Mission control is listening to a heartbeat too.
So the teams run tests. One at a time, carefully.
They command the stuck wheel to move.
And in one test, it does.
film.dir: breaking into a smile; stress 'it does'

film.vo: Whether it is truly recoverable, they don't know yet.
Odyssey is out of safe mode, but its science is still off.
The goal is science and relay back by late November.
Perseverance hopes to be back doing science by the end of the month.
So back to the hundred seconds of silence.
The rover did not break. It did what it was built to do.
It noticed the silence, swapped, and protected itself.
Out there, listening for a heartbeat is how you stay alive.
Which would you fix first, the rover or the orbiter?
Tell me in the comments.
Tomorrow: what if tonight's supermoon hung even closer?

short.vo: For one hundred seconds, a rover on Mars heard nothing.
Its radio stopped sending its heartbeat.
Twenty-five missed pings, and the computer pulled the plug.
It swapped to the backup radio and went into safe mode.
But the backup is only at half power.
So NASA parked both radios and talks straight to Earth.
Slower link, so science and photos are paused.
Meanwhile Odyssey, twenty-five years old, lost a wheel.
It needs three, and has fuel for one to two months without them.
One test, the wheel moved. NASA hopes both are back by month end.
Full film on the channel. Out there, silence is the scariest sound.
